title: Peetz Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Peetz wells have a 200-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $13,000-$23,000.
h1: What Peetz Well Records Tell You Before You Buy
intro_html:
Buying land near Peetz means evaluating the well, not just the house or acreage. Colorado DWR records show 133 permitted wells within five miles, with 89 recorded as constructed. Of those, 86 report a total depth, 39 report a pump yield, and 11 report a static water level.

The local records point to wells commonly completed in plains sedimentary rock or an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. Most reported wells produce useful flow, but the records are not a guarantee for an untested lot. Neighboring permits, the intended use, septic layout, and a driller’s site-specific opinion should all be part of your decision.

sections.heading: Peetz well depth: plan around the middle, not the outlier
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Peetz is 200 feet. The middle half runs from 142 to 260 feet, so a drilling bid based near that range is more grounded than one based on the deepest record. The 90th percentile is 410 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 560 feet.

Depth records are concentrated between 100 and 300 feet, accounting for 79% of the depth mix. Another 20% fall between 300 and 600 feet, while only 1% are under 100 feet. The spread reflects local changes in plains sediments and fractured rock. Ask a driller to review nearby logs before assuming your parcel will match the median.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Peetz
sections.html:
Among the 39 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 15.0 to 36.0 gallons per minute. That is a stronger reported yield profile than many buyers expect from a rural well, but a permit record is not the same as a current production test.

Seventy-seven percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 21% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 3% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. Confirm the actual yield, recovery, storage, and intended household or stock demand before closing.

sections.heading: Peetz water levels and what the records can show
sections.html:
The 11 wells reporting static water levels show a median depth to water of 92 feet. The middle half is relatively tight, from 80 to 100 feet. That gives a useful starting point for pump planning and for comparing nearby well logs, but it does not establish the water level at every property.

The permit totals by decade show activity in the 1960s, 1970s, 1980s, 1990s, 2000s, 2010s, and 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. The available facts do not pair enough water-level measurements with dates to demonstrate a dropping or rising water table. Have the seller provide current testing rather than relying on the median alone.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Peetz, and how recent is the record?
sections.html:
Permit activity near Peetz is spread across several decades. The records list 2 permits from the 1960s, 11 from the 1970s, 8 from the 1980s, 29 from the 1990s, 21 from the 2000s, 13 from the 2010s, and 15 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

In the recorded driller names, Stewart Drilling Co. (Stewart, Dennis W.) appears on 16 wells. M&S Drilling, Inc. (Monheiser, Mark) appears on 11, and M & S Drilling Inc. (Monheiser, Lawrence) on 10. These records can help identify local experience, but verify current licensing, availability, pricing, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new well may cost in the Peetz area
sections.html:
For Peetz ground described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 200 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $7,000 to $11,000.

A finished system costs more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the model puts a completed well near $13,000 to $23,000. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed bid. Confirm what casing, grout, mobilization, water testing, power work, and difficult access are included. A deeper-than-median hole or a change in formation can move the price outside the initial estimate.

sections.heading: Peetz risks: water quality, dry holes, and site layout
sections.html:
The records identify 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Peetz. They identify 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those facts do not certify a private well as safe. Test existing water for relevant contaminants, and ask the county or Colorado agencies whether a nearby site affects your parcel.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 122 wells in that category. Another 9 name the Ogallala and 1 names an alluvial aquifer. Fractured rock can be unpredictable, including the possibility of a low-yield or dry hole despite nearby success. Check casing, grout, pump setting, septic setbacks, drainage, and building access before finalizing a lot plan.

sections.heading: Buying or building between Peetz and nearby Logan County areas
sections.html:
Before buying, pull the neighboring permits and construction reports within the search area, then compare depth, aquifer name, static level, yield, and use. The same review is worthwhile around Padroni, Iliff, Crook, Sterling, Fleming, and Atwood when those places are part of your local comparison. A nearby well is evidence, not a promise for your parcel.

Confirm the permit allows the intended household, stock, or irrigation use. Colorado DWR rules matter, and an exempt household-use well still has limits, including the 35 gallons-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. For a build, coordinate the well, septic system, driveway, electrical route, and house location before drilling so one difficult site condition does not force expensive redesign.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Peetz, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported Peetz wells have a median depth of 200 feet. The middle half is between 142 and 260 feet. Most, or 79%, fall between 100 and 300 feet. However, the local record includes wells as deep as 560 feet, so nearby logs should guide the estimate for a specific parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Peetz?
faq.a: The drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 200-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $7,000 to $11,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,000 to $23,000. Get a written bid that states what is included.

faq.q: How much water do Peetz wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 39 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 15.0 to 36.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-seven percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. These are recorded results, not a guarantee for a new well, so require a production and recovery test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Peetz?
faq.a: The records show 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles. That does not establish the quality of an individual private well. Test the property’s water before purchase or occupancy, including contaminants recommended by local health officials. A permit, depth, or strong yield does not replace laboratory testing.

faq.q: What aquifer do wells near Peetz use?
faq.a: Permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 122 wells. The Ogallala is named for 9 wells, and the alluvial aquifer for 1. No wells in the records use a Denver Basin aquifer. Fractured-bedrock results can vary from one parcel to another, so compare neighboring logs and get a local driller’s assessment.
